nameStory: The 'Spurred Ridgeback' gets its name from the small spines or 'spurs' that stick out from ridges running along its back. These tiny projections give this little woodlouse a distinctly armored appearance, like a miniature dinosaur with a spiky backbone.
description: The Spurred Ridgeback is a small terrestrial isopod, commonly called a woodlouse or pillbug. This tiny crustacean typically measures just a few millimeters long and has an oval, segmented body that's grayish to brownish in color. Unlike some of its cousins, it cannot roll into a complete ball when threatened, instead relying on its speed and small size to escape predators.

idTips.label: Spurred ridges
idTips.description: Run your finger gently along the back - you'll feel tiny raised ridges with small spines or projections that give it a bumpy, textured feel

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Very small, usually 3-6mm long, with an elongated oval body that's about twice as long as it is wide

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Mottled gray to brown coloration, often with slightly darker patches along the segments, giving it good camouflage against soil

idTips.label: Rolling ability
idTips.description: Cannot roll into a tight ball like a pillbug - when disturbed, it will curl slightly but you'll still see gaps between its segments

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of antennae with the outer pair being noticeably longer and more prominent than the inner pair

habitat: Look for Spurred Ridgebacks in moist, protected areas under logs, stones, leaf litter, and in compost piles throughout New England. They prefer well-drained but humid microhabitats in deciduous and mixed forests, often near human settlements where they've established themselves since European colonization. You'll find them in garden beds, under mulch, and in basement window wells of older homes.

seasonality.spring: Active as soil warms, often found under lifting leaf litter and emerging vegetation. Look for them during mild, damp days when turning over stones or logs.
seasonality.summer: Most active during this season, especially after rain showers. They're easier to spot in early morning or evening when humidity is higher.
seasonality.fall: Still quite active, often congregating under fallen leaves and logs as they prepare for winter. This is when you're most likely to find multiple individuals together.
seasonality.winter: Much less active but can still be found under deep leaf litter or in protected spots like root cellars and basement areas where temperatures remain above freezing.

funFact: This tiny creature is actually a crustacean more closely related to lobsters and crabs than to insects - it even breathes through gill-like structures that must stay moist, which is why you'll never find one in a dry place!
confusionNotes: Often confused with common pillbugs (roly-polies), but remember: if it can roll into a perfect ball, it's not a Spurred Ridgeback. The ridgeback's spiny back texture and inability to fully curl up are dead giveaways.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'terrestrial cave isopod,' you're more likely to find this species in your garden than in actual caves in New England. The name refers to its preference for dark, cave-like microhabitats under rocks and logs rather than true cave dwelling.
compareHints: Since this is the only Haplophthalmus species commonly found in New England, compare it to other small woodlice in the Trichoniscidae family by looking for those distinctive spurred ridges on the back. Most other small isopods in the region lack these prominent spiny projections and have smoother, more rounded backs.
